newsitem.title: UK: S&P gives Astor B plus corporate credit rating.
newsitem.headline: S&P gives Astor B plus corporate credit rating.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Wednesday it assigned its B plus corporate credit rating to Astor Corp and its B minus rating to the company's $110 million senior subordinated notes due 2006, to be sold under Rule 144A.
The outlook was stable, S&P said.

"The initial ratings of Astor Corp reflect its aggressive financial management, heavy debt burden, and below-average business position as a niche specialty chemical producer. The company has a limited operating history, since Astor's predecessor emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy in June 1995," S&P said.
New management has implemented an aggressive growth strategy that will focus on producing a more diverse and value-added business mix, S&P said.
To that end, the June 1995 purchase of Associated British Industries Ltd for about $60 million added a British-based specialty waxes, adhesives, and sealants business to Astor's portfolio, S&P said.

The pending, similarly-sized acquisition of ADCO Technologies Inc. will add a profitable producer of adhesives and sealants used in applications such as roofing, automotive windshields, window manufacturing, and concrete pipe, S&P said.

These two entities, which comprise about 70 percent of pro forma revenues and around 75 percent of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), have shown decent profitability in recent years, demonstrating a resilience to fluctuations in petroleum-based feedstock costs.
Still, Astor remains exposed to cyclical end markets, and it also competes with some larger and financially stronger firms.
Astor is highly leveraged, with a debt/EBITDA ratio of nearly five times after the ADCO acquisition.

The firm is expected to use modest free cash flow plus moderate additional debt to make "bolt-on" acquisitions. In addition to its debt service requirements, Astor could at some point choose to refinance 14.5 percent pay-in-kind preferred stock of its parent company (face value currently about $25 million), S&P said.

"These concerns underpin expectations of continued thin interest coverage, weak cash flow protection, and aggressive debt leverage. Liquidity is provided by a six-year $30 million bank revolver, and debt maturities are manageable until the revolver matures," S&P said.
"Though financial flexibility is somewhat constrained, rating prospects are stabilised by an improving cost position and increasing value-added product mix," S&P said.
